etymology: From wine and the old verb bib, “to drink,” from the Latin bibere, “to drink”; hence a wine-drinker, a tippler, one habitually given to the cup — a drunkard.
biblical_def: A winebibber is a wine-drinker — one who tipples, who tarries over the cup, a drunkard. The word joins wine to the old verb bib, and it names not the man who tastes but the man who cannot leave off. Solomon sets him among the company a wise son must shun: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh” (Pro 23:20), “for the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21). The father draws the portrait whole — “Who hath woe? who hath sorrow?… They that tarry long at the wine” (Pro 23:29–30) — and bids the son not so much as look upon it when it is red. Isaiah pronounces the woe over it: “Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink” (Isa 5:11). Yet the sharpest use of the word is a slander flung at the Son of God. Christ came eating and drinking, and the scribes sneered, “Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners” (Mat 11:19; cf. Luk 7:34). He was no winebibber; He was holy, harmless, undefiled. But He would sit at a publican’s table to save a publican, and the self-righteous had no name for such mercy but a drunkard’s name. The LORD who was falsely called a winebibber is the LORD who delivers the true one.
webster_summary: A wine-drinker; a tippler; one habitually given to wine — a drunkard.
webster_full: WINEBIBBER, one who drinks much wine; a tippler; a drunkard.
From wine and bib, “to drink,” from the Latin bibere.
It names not the taster but the man who tarries long at the cup.
Solomon warns, Be not among winebibbers (Pro 23:20).
The scribes falsely called Christ a winebibber (Mat 11:19).
scriptures: Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:
The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.
Luk 7:34
The Son of man is come eating and drinking; and ye say, Behold a gluttonous man, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners!
For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
corruption_summary: An old, plain word for the drunkard; and the drunkard is no antique figure, for our age has made the cup a personality and a comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: The live sin to name is the age’s easy friendship with the bottle. Drunkenness is no longer thought a vice but a style: the daily glass held up as a personality, the wine poured to bear the day, the joke that a mother cannot mind her children without it, the young man who measures his manhood by how much he can hold. Scripture is not fooled by the packaging. It counts the winebibber with the glutton and sends both to poverty and rags; it asks who has woe and sorrow and wounds without cause, and answers, they that tarry long at the wine. What the world calls unwinding, the LORD calls a snare, and He warns the son not to look upon the wine when it is red, for the taste that seems harmless is the door to the habit that clothes a man with rags.

The grace that mortifies this sin is not the pledge of the moralist but the fulness of the Spirit. Paul does not merely forbid the cup; he offers a better filling: “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). The winebibber drinks to fill an emptiness the wine cannot fill; the answer is a soul filled with Christ, that has no room left for the excess. And there is comfort here for the man already in the ditch: the very name flung as a slander at the sinless Christ is the pledge of his rescue, for the LORD who was called a friend of publicans and sinners is exactly the friend a winebibber needs. He came eating and drinking with such men to save them, and He saves them still.
roots_summary: The word means a wine-drinker, a tippler, one habitually given to the cup.
roots_lines: Winebibber — wine + bib, “to drink,” from Latin bibere.
It names the habitual drinker, not the man who merely tastes.
Solomon ranks him with the riotous eater of flesh (Pro 23:20).
His end is poverty, drowsiness, and rags (Pro 23:21).
The word was flung as a slander at Christ Himself (Mat 11:19).
usage: Be not among winebibbers: the wise man shuns the company of the cup.
A winebibber is not the man who tastes wine but the man who cannot leave it.
They called Christ a winebibber — the sinless One who ate with sinners to save them.

etymology: From the Old French surfaire, “to overdo, to overload” (sur, “over,” + faire, “to do,” from Latin facere); hence excess in eating and drinking, and the heaviness, nausea, and stupor that follow gluttonous overindulgence.
biblical_def: Surfeiting is the sickness of excess — the heaviness and stupor that follow gorging and overdrinking, the body and soul overloaded past their measure. The word appears once, and it falls from the lips of the LORD Himself in His warning about the last day: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares” (Luk 21:34). Mark the peril He names. The danger is not only the drunkard’s grosser sin but the dull, overcharged heart — the soul so weighed down with feasting and fretting that it cannot watch, and is taken unawares when the Son of man comes. Surfeiting deadens; it is the enemy of vigilance. So Paul commands the day-walk that has no room for it: “Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness” (Rom 13:13); and against the false fulness of the cup he sets the true: “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). Peter buries it in the Gentile past, “when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings” (1Pe 4:3). The believer is a watchman, sober and awake, for “let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober” (1Th 5:6). The overcharged heart cannot keep the vigil the LORD requires.
webster_summary: Excess in eating and drinking; the heaviness and stupor that follow gluttonous overindulgence.
webster_full: SURFEITING, excess in eating and drinking; oppression of the body by intemperance.
From Old French surfaire, “to overdo,” sur (“over”) + faire (“to do”).
It names not the meal but the overloading of it — the glutton’s stupor.
Christ warns of hearts overcharged with surfeiting (Luk 21:34).
It deadens the soul and unfits it to watch for its Lord.
scriptures: And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
corruption_summary: An archaic word for the glutton’s excess; the word has faded, but the sin has been enthroned by an age of appetite without limit.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear does not know the word, and the modern age has lost the sin that named it. Gluttony was once counted among the deadly sins; now it is a market. We are surrounded by surfeiting made a virtue — the endless plenty, the meal that never ends, the counsel to indulge and treat oneself as though restraint were a cruelty. But Christ did not warn against surfeiting because gorging is unmannerly; He warned because the overcharged heart cannot watch. The soul that is always feeding is always dull, and the day of the LORD comes upon the drowsy unawares. An age that cannot fast has forgotten how to be sober, and a church that mirrors it will be found sleeping when the Bridegroom comes.

The grace that mortifies surfeiting is sober watchfulness under the Spirit’s fulness. The remedy is not merely a smaller plate but a filled soul: he who is filled with the Spirit is not overcharged with the world. Scripture bids the saint keep the day-walk — honest, awake, unweighted by rioting or by the cares that clog the heart as surely as the feast does. The Christian holds his appetites with a loose hand because he is looking for a coming, and a man watching for his Lord will not gorge himself into a stupor at the gate. Temperance is not the enemy of joy but its guardian: the sober heart tastes every good gift as a mercy and worships none of them, and so is ready, whatever the hour, when the Son of man comes.
roots_summary: The word means excess in eating and drinking, and the stupor that follows it.
roots_lines: Surfeiting — Old French surfaire, “to overdo, to overload.”
From sur (“over”) + faire (“to do”), from Latin facere.
It names the overloading of the meal, not the meal itself.
A KJV hapax: hearts overcharged with surfeiting (Luk 21:34).
Its fruit is a dull heart, unfit to watch for the LORD.
usage: Surfeiting is not the meal but the gorging of it — excess that deadens the soul.
Take heed lest your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting: the full heart cannot watch.
The sober believer holds his appetite with a loose hand, looking for his Lord’s return.

etymology: From the Old French reveler, “to make riot, to rebel,” from the Latin rebellare, “to rebel”; hence riotous festivity, noisy carousing — the loud, lawless merrymaking of the drunken feast.
biblical_def: Revelling is riotous carousing — the loud, unbridled merrymaking of the drunken feast, the carousal that spills into the street. The word is twinned with rebellion in its very root, and Scripture always names it among the works of the flesh. Paul lists it in the catalogue that bars a man from the kingdom: “Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before… that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal 5:21). Peter numbers it with the works of the buried past: “when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries” (1Pe 4:3). And Paul sets it against the walk of the day: “Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying” (Rom 13:13). Note that revelling never travels alone; it comes in with drunkenness on one arm and wantonness on the other, and the idols close behind. The reveller has made a feast his god and his belly his altar — “whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame” (Php 3:19). Against the false, roaring fulness of the carousal the apostle sets the true and quiet fulness of the Spirit: “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). There are two intoxications and two kingdoms; the revelling that shall not inherit the one is answered by the sober joy of the other.
webster_summary: Riotous festivity; noisy carousing; the loud, lawless merrymaking of the drunken feast.
webster_full: REVELLING, riotous carousing; noisy and disorderly feasting; wanton merrymaking.
From Old French reveler, “to make riot,” from Latin rebellare, “to rebel.”
Its very root is rebellion — feasting that has thrown off all rule.
Paul lists it among the works of the flesh (Gal 5:21).
Peter buries it in the Gentile past (1Pe 4:3).
scriptures: Gal 5:21
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
corruption_summary: An old word for the drunken carousal; the thing itself is the beating heart of a hedonist age that lives for the party and the night.
corruption_paragraphs: The live sin is the enthronement of the revel. Our age does not hide its carousing; it advertises it. The weekend exists for it, the music industry sells it, the young are taught that the loud, drunken, lawless night is the summit of a life — and the man who will not join is pitied. Scripture calls this rebellion by its name, for the very root of the word is rebellion, and it sets revelling among the works of the flesh that shut a man out of the kingdom of God. The reveller thinks himself free; he is a rebel with a cup in his hand, worshipping his own appetite. And the apostle who lists the sin adds the sober warning that those who make a life of it “shall not inherit the kingdom of God” — a sentence the party never reads aloud.

The grace that answers revelling is a better feast and a truer fulness. Paul does not merely tear the cup from the reveller’s hand; he offers a joy the carousal only counterfeits: “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.” There are two intoxications. The one leaves a man empty, ashamed, and shut out; the other fills him with a gladness that needs no morning to regret. The Christian is not a man robbed of mirth but a man given the real thing — the joy of the LORD that is his strength, the sober delight of a table where Christ is host. The reveller runs to the night to forget; the believer walks in the day, honest and awake, and finds his feast is only beginning.
roots_summary: The word means riotous carousing — the noisy, lawless merrymaking of the drunken feast.
roots_lines: Revelling — Old French reveler, “to make riot,” from Latin rebellare.
Its root is rebellare, “to rebel” — feasting that throws off rule.
It denotes the drunken carousal, loud and disorderly.
Paul bars the reveller from the kingdom of God (Gal 5:21).
It travels with drunkenness, wantonness, and idolatry (1Pe 4:3).
usage: Revelling is the drunken carousal — and its very root is rebellion against God.
They which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom: the party does not read that line.
Against the roar of the revel the apostle sets the quiet fulness of the Spirit.

etymology: From the Old French railler, “to mock, to jest bitterly,” perhaps from a Vulgar Latin ragulare, “to bray”; hence abusive, reviling speech — scoffing and insult, the reproachful tongue that reviles rather than reasons.
biblical_def: Railing is reviling speech — abuse, insult, the scoffing tongue that reproaches instead of reasoning. It is the language of the proud and empty man. Paul traces it to its root in the false teacher who “is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings” (1Ti 6:4). Where sound doctrine fails, the tongue turns to insult. Peter forbids the saint to answer in kind: “Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing” (1Pe 3:9). The Christian breaks the chain, returning a blessing for a curse. The gravest railing in Scripture was flung at the crucified Christ, “and they that passed by railed on him, wagging their heads” (Mar 15:29) — the King of glory reviled by the men He came to save, and He reviled not again. So terrible a sin is a railing accusation that even the archangel would not stoop to it against the devil himself: “Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil… durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee” (Jud 1:9). If Michael would not rail on Satan, what shall be said of the brother who rails on a brother? Paul puts the railer out of the fellowship, naming him with “a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat” (1Co 5:11). The reviling tongue has no place at the LORD’s table.
webster_summary: Abusive, reviling speech; scoffing and insult; the reproachful tongue that reviles rather than reasons.
webster_full: RAILING, reproachful or insolent language; the utterance of abuse or reviling.
From Old French railler, “to mock, to jest bitterly.”
It is the tongue of the proud man when his argument fails.
Peter forbids rendering railing for railing (1Pe 3:9).
The passers-by railed on the crucified Christ (Mar 15:29).
scriptures: He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings,
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
Jud 1:9
Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.
And they that passed by railed on him, wagging their heads, and saying, Ah, thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days,
corruption_summary: An old word for the reviling tongue, and never more at home than now, when the insult has become a public sport and outrage a way of life.
corruption_paragraphs: The live sin is the railing tongue enthroned as public discourse. The age has built whole platforms for it: the comment thread, the mob that gathers to revile, the pile-on that hunts a man’s reputation for pleasure, the pundit whose whole trade is the sneer. It is exactly what Paul described — men proud, knowing nothing, doting about strifes of words, out of which comes envy, strife, and railings. Where the mind has no argument, the mouth has an insult, and a generation that has forgotten how to reason has learned instead how to revile. The church is not exempt: brethren who would never strike a man will rail on him from a distance, and the tongue that Michael would not turn against the devil is turned freely against a brother over a disagreement.

The grace that mortifies railing is the cross-shaped tongue that blesses the reviler. Peter’s command is not merely to hold the peace but to break the chain: not railing for railing, but contrariwise blessing. The Christian has a pattern he cannot escape — the King of glory railed on as He hung, wagging heads and mocking mouths beneath Him, and He reviled not again, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously. The servant is not above his Master. To answer scorn with a blessing is not weakness but the deepest strength, for it is the imitation of Christ crucified, and it comes with a promise: they are called to it that they should inherit a blessing. The railer spends his tongue and gains a curse; the saint holds his and inherits a blessing.
roots_summary: The word means reviling, abusive speech — scoffing and insult in place of reason.
roots_lines: Railing — Old French railler, “to mock, to jest bitterly.”
It denotes reviling, reproachful, insolent speech.
It is the tongue of the proud man when his doctrine fails (1Ti 6:4).
Michael durst not bring a railing accusation against the devil (Jud 1:9).
The saint is forbidden to render railing for railing (1Pe 3:9).
usage: Railing is reviling, not reasoning — the insult of the man whose argument has failed.
Not railing for railing, but contrariwise blessing: the Christian breaks the chain.
Even Michael durst not rail on Satan; what then of the brother who rails on a brother?

etymology: From the Latin clamor, “a shout, an outcry,” from clamare, “to cry out”; hence loud, angry outcry — the raised, brawling voice of contention.
biblical_def: Clamour is loud, angry outcry — the raised voice of quarrel, the brawling noise of a heart out of rule. Paul lists it in the cluster of tongue-sins the new man must strip off: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice” (Eph 4:31). Mark the company it keeps — bitterness within, wrath and anger rising, clamour breaking out at the mouth, evil speaking, and malice at the bottom of all. Clamour is anger gone audible; it is the shout that a governed spirit would have swallowed. Wisdom is quiet, but “a foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing” (Pro 9:13). The remedy is the discipline of the ear and the tongue: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” (Jas 1:19). The swift hearer and slow speaker raises no clamour, for he has taken the heat off the coal before it can flame. And Solomon knew the power of the lowered voice against the raised: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger” (Pro 15:1). Clamour answers clamour and the fire climbs; the soft answer starves it. The man who has “no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls” (Pro 25:28), and every clamour is a breach in the wall. The Spirit builds the wall again in meekness, and the loud man learns at last to be still.
webster_summary: Loud and angry outcry; the raised, brawling voice of contention.
webster_full: CLAMOUR, a great outcry; loud and continued noise; vociferation, as of a quarrel.
From the Latin clamor, “a shout,” from clamare, “to cry out.”
In Scripture it is anger gone audible — the shout a governed spirit swallows.
Paul bids the saint put away all clamour (Eph 4:31).
The foolish woman is clamorous, and knoweth nothing (Pro 9:13).
scriptures: Eph 4:31
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
Pro 9:13
A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
corruption_summary: The KJV counts clamour a sin to be put away; the modern tongue counts it a virtue, for we now clamour for our rights and mistake the loudest voice for the truest.
corruption_paragraphs: There is an honest drift in the word worth naming: today “to clamour” simply means to demand something loudly, and the demanding is thought a good thing — we clamour for reform, for rights, for our due, and admire the crowd that shouts the loudest. The Authorized Version knows no such approval. It sets clamour among bitterness, wrath, anger, evil speaking, and malice, and commands the saint to put it away with the rest. The instinct of the age is the reverse: it teaches that the wronged should raise their voices, that the squeaking wheel is oiled, that volume is a kind of righteousness. But Scripture measures the tongue not by its loudness but by its rule, and the loud, brawling outcry is a work of the old man, whatever cause it wears.

The grace that answers clamour is the governed spirit and the soft answer. James gives the discipline — swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath — and Solomon the weapon: a soft answer turneth away wrath, while grievous words only stir the fire higher. The man ruled by the Spirit does not need to shout, for he is not defending a throne of self that every slight endangers; he can be wronged and stay quiet, corrected and stay kind. The clamorous heart is a city broken down and without walls, at the mercy of every provocation; the meek heart is walled and at peace. Christ, led as a lamb to the slaughter, opened not His mouth — and the loudest room is often the one furthest from Him.
roots_summary: The word means loud, angry outcry — the brawling voice of a heart out of rule.
roots_lines: Clamour — Latin clamor, “a shout,” from clamare, “to cry out.”
It denotes loud, continued, angry outcry — vociferation.
It is anger made audible, the shout a governed spirit swallows.
Paul lists it among the tongue-sins to be put away (Eph 4:31).
The soft answer, not the loud, turns away wrath (Pro 15:1).
usage: Clamour is anger gone audible — the shout a ruled spirit would have swallowed.
The KJV bids us put away clamour; the age bids us clamour for our rights.
A soft answer turneth away wrath: the lowered voice starves the fire the raised one feeds.

etymology: From the Middle Dutch and Middle English tatelen, “to prate, to chatter,” of imitative origin; hence an idle talker, a prater, one who tells what should not be told — a gossip and busybody.
biblical_def: A tattler is an idle prater — one whose tongue runs where it should be still, carrying tales from house to house and telling what ought never to be told. Paul names the sin in the younger widows who, left without useful labour, “learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” (1Ti 5:13). Note the pedigree of the sin: idleness first, then wandering, then the busy tongue — the empty hour breeds the meddling word. Solomon warns against keeping such company: “He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips” (Pro 20:19). The tattler cannot hold a confidence; what he hears, he spends. And the tale, once loosed, is fuel: “Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth” (Pro 26:20). Take away the tattler and the quarrel dies for want of feeding. Behind all these stands the law of the LORD, which forbids the wandering tongue outright: “Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD” (Lev 19:16). The tattler thinks his words small coin, but “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Pro 18:21). What he scatters idly, God will weigh.
webster_summary: An idle talker; a prater; one who tells tales and secrets that should not be told — a gossip.
webster_full: TATTLER, one who prates; a telltale; an idle talker; one who reveals secrets.
From tatelen, “to prate, to chatter,” of imitative origin.
Its pedigree is idleness, then wandering, then the meddling tongue.
Paul names the tattling, busybody widows (1Ti 5:13).
The law forbids going up and down as a talebearer (Lev 19:16).
scriptures: And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.
He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.
corruption_summary: An old word for the busy, meddling tongue; and the tattler now has instruments the ancient world never dreamed of, and calls his prating news.
corruption_paragraphs: The live sin is the tattler armed with a glowing screen. What Paul described — the idle who wander from house to house, speaking things they ought not — now travels at the speed of light and never leaves the chair. The feed of another’s troubles, the group chat that dissects a neighbour, the “prayer request” that is a confidence broken, the whole culture of oversharing that treats a private matter as public entertainment: these are the wandering tongue given wings. The age even flatters it, calling gossip “news” and idle meddling “keeping informed.” But Scripture strips the disguise. It roots the sin in idleness, warns that the talebearer reveals secrets, and forbids the saint to go up and down as one, for the tongue that will not keep a confidence will not keep a covenant either.

The grace that mortifies the tattler is the disciplined tongue that starves a quarrel and keeps a trust. Solomon gives the picture: where no wood is, the fire goes out, and where there is no talebearer, the strife ceases. Half the church’s conflicts would die overnight if no one carried the fuel. The Christian is called to be the man who withholds the wood — who covers a matter in love, who lets a confidence die with him, whose diligent hands leave no idle hour for the busy tongue to fill. And behind the whole duty stands the awful weight the tattler forgets: death and life are in the power of the tongue, and the God who signs His law “I am the LORD” will weigh every idle word. The remedy for a light tongue is a heavy sense of that reckoning.
roots_summary: The word means an idle prater, a gossip, one who tells what ought not to be told.
roots_lines: Tattler — from tatelen, “to prate, to chatter,” of imitative origin.
It denotes an idle talker, a telltale, a revealer of secrets.
Its pedigree: idleness, then wandering, then the meddling word (1Ti 5:13).
The talebearer reveals secrets; meddle not with him (Pro 20:19).
The law forbids going up and down as a talebearer (Lev 19:16).
usage: A tattler is the idle prater whose tongue runs where it should be still.
Where there is no talebearer the strife ceases: the tattler is the fire’s fuel.
The tattler thinks his words small coin; death and life are in the power of the tongue.

etymology: From the Old English strīcan, “to strike, to go, to stroke”; here in the plain sense of one who strikes blows — a violent, pugnacious man, quick with his fists, expressly disqualified from the oversight of the church.
biblical_def: A striker is a violent man — one quick to blows, ready with his fists, a brawler whose anger goes straight to his hand. The word stands twice in Scripture, and both times in the roll of what an elder must not be. To Timothy: a bishop must be “not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous” (1Ti 3:3). To Titus, of the same office: “not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre” (Tit 1:7). The man who leads Christ’s flock may not be a man of his fists; the shepherd’s crook is not a cudgel. The reason lies deeper than the office, for the servant of the LORD as such is forbidden strife: “the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24). Gentleness, not force, is the mark of the man of God. And the wise man warns that a violent temper is catching, so that even the striker’s company is a snare: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go; lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul” (Pro 22:24–25). The striker answers injury with a blow; the Christian answers it as his Master did, “who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not” (1Pe 2:23). The gospel unclenches the fist.
webster_summary: A violent, pugnacious man, quick to blows — expressly disqualified from the office of a bishop.
webster_full: STRIKER, one who strikes; a violent, quarrelsome man ready with his fists.
From Old English strīcan, “to strike,” in the sense of dealing blows.
It names the pugnacious temper whose anger runs straight to the hand.
A bishop must be no striker, but patient (1Ti 3:3).
The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle (2Ti 2:24).
scriptures: Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;
Tit 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go:
corruption_summary: A plain word for the violent man, and one the church still needs, for the fist and the flaring temper have not gone out of the world or out of the pew.
corruption_paragraphs: The live sin is the violence the world excuses and the church too often overlooks. The striker is the man quick to the fist — the bully, the brawler, the husband whose anger goes to his hand, the leader who rules by intimidation and calls it strength. Our age is confused about him. It celebrates aggression as manliness on the screen while professing to abhor it, and it will hand a forceful, domineering man authority in the church because he “gets things done,” the very disqualification Paul names notwithstanding. Scripture is not confused. Twice it bars the striker from the eldership by name, and it warns every believer to make no friendship with an angry man, lest his ways prove catching and become a snare to the soul. A violent temper is not a strong leadership style; it is a mark of a man not yet fit to lead.

The grace that mortifies the striker is the gentleness of Christ. The servant of the LORD must not strive but be gentle unto all men, patient, apt to teach — and the pattern is the Master Himself, who when He was reviled reviled not again, and when He suffered threatened not, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously. Here is the miracle the gospel works: it takes the clenched fist and opens it. The man who once answered every injury with a blow learns to answer it with a blessing, to bear wrong rather than avenge it, to lead by the shepherd’s patience and not the striker’s force. This is no weakness; it is the strength of a spirit ruled, for he that is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
roots_summary: The word means a violent, pugnacious man, quick to blows — unfit for the oversight of the church.
roots_lines: Striker — Old English strīcan, “to strike,” to deal a blow.
It names the pugnacious man whose anger goes straight to his hand.
Twice it is set among the disqualifications of a bishop (1Ti 3:3; Tit 1:7).
The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle (2Ti 2:24).
Make no friendship with an angry man, lest it snare thy soul (Pro 22:24).
usage: A striker is a man of his fists — and Scripture bars him from the eldership by name.
No striker: the shepherd’s crook is not a cudgel, and force is no fitness to lead.
The gospel unclenches the fist, teaching the striker his Master reviled not again.

etymology: From high + minded — but the KJV never means noble or lofty in the good sense. It renders the Greek for “puffed up, conceited”; hence proud, arrogant, swollen with self-esteem.
biblical_def: Highminded in the KJV does not mean noble or magnanimous, as the modern ear takes it. It means proud — swollen, conceited, lifted up with self-esteem. The word renders the Greek for a mind puffed above its measure, and Scripture uses it always as a rebuke. To the Gentile church grafted into Israel’s olive, Paul gives the sharpest warning against boasting over the branches broken off: “because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear” (Rom 11:20). The grafted branch has nothing it did not receive; let it tremble rather than swell. He charges the rich the same: “that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God” (1Ti 6:17) — for riches are the great fuel of a high mind, and they take wings. And among the marks of the perilous last days he sets it in dreadful company: “Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God” (2Ti 3:4). The high mind loves itself and its pleasures, and God not at all. Against all this stands the fixed law of heaven: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18), and “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jas 4:6). The remedy is not a low opinion falsely worn but a true one: “Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate” (Rom 12:16). The highminded man stands by faith and forgets it; the humble man stands by faith and fears.
webster_summary: Proud, arrogant, conceited — not noble, as the modern ear supposes, but swollen with self.
webster_full: HIGHMINDED, proud; arrogant; puffed up with a conceit of oneself.
From high and minded; it renders the Greek for “puffed up.”
The KJV never means noble or lofty in a good sense, as we now do.
The grafted Gentile is charged, Be not highminded, but fear (Rom 11:20).
The rich are charged the same, lest riches take wings (1Ti 6:17).
scriptures: Well; because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear:
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
corruption_summary: A word turned inside out: the KJV’s highminded man is a proud man, but our age has made high-mindedness a compliment and self-esteem a gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a genuine reversal, and a live corruption behind it. The KJV’s highminded man is the proud man, the swollen man, puffed above his measure; but the modern ear hears the word as praise — the high-minded man is the noble idealist, and to think highly of oneself has become the first duty of mental health. The age preaches a whole gospel of self-esteem: love yourself, believe in yourself, silence the inner critic, for your problem is that you have thought too little of yourself, never too much. Scripture teaches the exact reverse. It names highmindedness among the marks of the perilous last days, alongside the traitor and the lover of pleasure; it charges the grafted branch and the rich man alike not to swell; and it warns that pride goes before destruction. What our therapists prescribe, the apostles proscribe.

The grace that answers highmindedness is the fear of a branch that knows it was grafted. Paul’s cure is not self-hatred but truth: be not highminded, but fear — remember that thou standest by faith, that thou hast nothing thou didst not receive, that the God who grafted thee in can break thee off. God resisteth the proud but giveth grace to the humble, and so the swollen soul is exactly the one He opposes. The remedy is to mind not high things but to condescend to men of low estate, walking softly before a God who has been merciful. True humility is not thinking meanly of oneself; it is thinking of oneself less, and of the grace that saved a debtor more. The highminded stand by faith and forget it; the lowly stand by faith and tremble — and it is the trembling that keeps them standing.
roots_summary: The word means proud, arrogant, puffed up with self — the KJV sense, not the modern “noble.”
roots_lines: Highminded — high + minded, rendering the Greek for “puffed up.”
In the KJV it means proud and arrogant, never noble or lofty.
The grafted Gentile is warned, Be not highminded, but fear (Rom 11:20).
It stands among the marks of the perilous last days (2Ti 3:4).
Pride goes before destruction; God resisteth the proud (Pro 16:18; Jas 4:6).
usage: Highminded in the KJV means proud, not noble: the swollen mind, puffed above its measure.
Be not highminded, but fear: the grafted branch has nothing it did not receive.
The age preaches self-esteem; the apostle preaches the fear that keeps a man standing.

etymology: From the Latin lascivus, “wanton, lustful, unbridled”; hence unrestrained sensuality, wantonness — lust that has thrown off all shame and given itself over to filthy indulgence without check.
biblical_def: Lasciviousness is wantonness — unbridled lust, sensuality that has cast off all restraint and shame. It is not a single act but a disposition, the heart given over to filthy pleasure and careless who knows it. Paul heads the works of the flesh with it: “the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness” (Gal 5:19), and warns that “they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal 5:21). Christ traces it to its true fountain, the heart, listing it among the things that come from within and defile the man — “covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye” (Mar 7:22). It is not the world that corrupts a clean heart; it is the heart that pours out its own filth. Peter numbers it with the buried Gentile past, “when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine” (1Pe 4:3). Its most fearful description is Paul’s, for it names a conscience seared past shame: men “being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness” (Eph 4:19). Mark the words — past feeling, given over, with greediness. Lasciviousness is lust that has stopped struggling and started feeding. Against it stands the crucifixion of the flesh: “they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal 5:24), and the daily command, “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” (Col 3:5). The gospel does not manage this sin; it kills it.
webster_summary: Wantonness; unbridled lust; unrestrained sensuality that has cast off all shame.
webster_full: LASCIVIOUSNESS, wantonness; lewdness; unrestrained indulgence of lust.
From the Latin lascivus, “wanton, lustful, unbridled.”
It is not a single act but a disposition of the heart given over to filth.
Paul heads the works of the flesh with it (Gal 5:19).
The past-feeling give themselves over unto it with greediness (Eph 4:19).
scriptures: Gal 5:19
Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness,
Mar 7:22
Thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness:
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Eph 4:19
Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.
corruption_summary: A word for wantonness under a live and open corruption: the age has made what Paul calls a work of the flesh into a badge of freedom and a public celebration.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption here is plain and must be named: our age has taken lasciviousness — the very word Paul heads the works of the flesh with — and rebranded it as liberation. What Scripture calls wantonness the culture calls “sex-positivity”; what Paul calls a conscience past feeling the world calls being free of shame; what Peter buries in the Gentile past is paraded as the mark of an enlightened present. Entertainment is saturated with it, advertising trades on it, and the young are catechized from childhood that appetite is identity and restraint is repression. But renaming a sin does not unmake it. Paul says without flinching that they which do such things “shall not inherit the kingdom of God,” and he describes the very state the age holds up as freedom — men past feeling, given over, working all uncleanness with greediness — as the deepest bondage a soul can know. A conscience that has stopped hurting is not healed; it is seared.

The grace that mortifies lasciviousness is the cross applied to the flesh and the fountain cleansed. Christ located the filth where it truly lives — not in the world outside but in the heart, whence it proceeds and defiles the man — so the remedy must reach the heart, and only the gospel does. They that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts; the believer does not merely restrain this sin but is commanded to slay it: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth.” This is no counsel of despair, for the same grace that condemns the sin has washed the sinner — “And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified.” The wanton heart, given over to feeding, is not managed by willpower or excused by the age; it is put to death by the Spirit and made clean by the blood, and the freedom it counterfeited is found at last in purity.
roots_summary: The word means wantonness, unbridled lust — sensuality that has cast off all shame.
roots_lines: Lasciviousness — Latin lascivus, “wanton, lustful, unbridled.”
It denotes not a single act but a disposition given over to filth.
Paul heads the works of the flesh with it (Gal 5:19).
Christ traces it to the heart, whence it defiles the man (Mar 7:22).
The past-feeling give themselves to it with greediness (Eph 4:19).
usage: Lasciviousness is wantonness — lust that has stopped struggling and started feeding.
The age calls it freedom; Paul calls it a work of the flesh that bars the kingdom.
They that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh: the gospel kills this sin, not manages it.

etymology: From the Latin novicius, “newly come, new,” from novus, “new”; hence a new convert, one newly planted in the faith — a beginner not yet grounded, and not to be set over the church.
biblical_def: A novice is a new convert — one newly planted in the faith, a beginner not yet grounded or proved. The Latin novus, “new,” is its whole root, and Paul uses the word to fence the highest office of the church. Among the qualifications of a bishop he sets this: “Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1Ti 3:6). The danger is precise. Give a raw convert the honour of rule before his character is tried, and the honour will swell him; he will be lifted up with pride and fall as the devil fell, by the very same sin. Newness of grace is no reproach — every saint was once new — but newness is not readiness, and the church that hurries a man into office does him a cruelty. So Paul charges Timothy to ordain slowly: “Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men’s sins; keep thyself pure” (1Ti 5:22). Eldership is proved, not presumed; Titus was to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) from among the tested. Yet the opposite error is real too, for the writer to the Hebrews rebukes those who stay novices: “when for the time ye ought to be teachers… have need of milk, and not of strong meat” (Heb 5:12). The flock is fed by proven men, whom the Holy Ghost has made “overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).
webster_summary: A new convert; a beginner in the faith, not yet grounded, and not to be set over the church.
webster_full: NOVICE, one new in any business; here, a new convert to the faith.
From the Latin novicius, from novus, “new.”
Newness of grace is no reproach, but newness is not readiness.
A bishop must be no novice, lest pride destroy him (1Ti 3:6).
Ordain slowly: lay hands suddenly on no man (1Ti 5:22).
scriptures: Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil.
Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins: keep thyself pure.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Heb 5:12

For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
corruption_summary: The plain word for a new convert; and the danger Paul fenced against is exactly the one a celebrity age courts, hurrying the newly famous into the pulpit.
corruption_paragraphs: The live sin is the church’s hunger to platform the new and the notable. Paul forbade a novice the eldership, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil; and the age does precisely what he forbade. The famous convert — the athlete, the entertainer, the influencer newly professing — is handed a stage before his character is tried, made a teacher of the church while he still needs teaching, and set up to fall by the very sin that felled Satan. The instinct is understandable and disastrous: a name draws a crowd, and a crowd is mistaken for a calling. But Scripture measures a man for office not by his following but by his proving, and to lift a novice into rule is to load a green branch with fruit it cannot bear. Many a public shipwreck of a young celebrity Christian is simply this sin come home.

The grace to recover is the patience of the proving church and the diligence of the growing saint. Paul’s rule cuts two ways. To the church: lay hands suddenly on no man, ordain from among the tested, and be in no haste to crown a convert, for eldership is proved, not presumed. And to every believer: do not remain a novice. The Hebrews are rebuked because, when for the time they ought to have been teachers, they still needed milk and not strong meat — newness excused at first becomes a reproach when it is chosen. The healthy soul grows: it moves from milk to meat, from being taught to teaching, and offers itself to be proved in the lowly things before it is trusted with the high. The flock is fed by men the Holy Ghost has made overseers and the years have made ready, over a church purchased with blood too precious to hand to the untried.
roots_summary: The word means a new convert, a beginner not yet grounded, not to be set over the church.
roots_lines: Novice — Latin novicius, from novus, “new.”
It denotes one newly planted in the faith, not yet proved.
A bishop must be no novice, lest pride destroy him (1Ti 3:6).
Eldership is proved, not presumed: lay hands suddenly on no man (1Ti 5:22).
Yet the convert who will not grow is rebuked too (Heb 5:12).
usage: A novice is a new convert — new in grace, but newness is not readiness to rule.
Not a novice, lest pride destroy him: a name is not a calling.
The flock is fed by proven men over a church purchased with blood.
